name: Priya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and have worked the customer calls and chats for years. I finished secondary school and handle the usual account questions about as well as my colleagues. I use AI every day to sort long notes, then check the bill myself, because a fluent answer can still be wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you carry home from work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tarek works as a hospital porter, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. I am paid at the low end of this job, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few other centres nearby, so I can be curious about a tool and still be scared of losing this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team a small AI saving is useful if it gives us time to check a bill. I would show the agents how to compare a draft with the original account note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my job to stay, but my pay does not leave much after the mortgage and school costs. Tarek's hospital shifts vary, and our reserve is less than a month. I cannot call that secure even if AI stays modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep answering the account queue and checking each AI draft against the original note. I would take one wrong draft to the monthly staff meeting and put a small fixed amount into savings on payday. In the first year we would keep our old dining table instead of replacing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household, not about a tiny software change. A tool can save a minute, but it cannot pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was wrong in that draft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It said a fee had been refunded when the account only showed a request. I caught it before sending, but someone else might have trusted the smooth wording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tarek agree to keep the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. It wobbles, but a folded card fixes it for dinner. Tarek would rather have one more mortgage payment set aside.

I would show agents the **original note** before trusting drafts.
think: Our **thin reserve** and variable hospital shifts still worry me even if AI stays modest.
do: Keep checking **AI drafts** against account notes.
Bring a wrong **refund draft** to the staff meeting.
Save a little and keep the old **table**.

fieldNote: She uses AI **daily** but spots smooth false refund claims.
The table delay protects a small **mortgage reserve**.

steps.text: Keep answering account chats and check AI drafts against original notes
Transfer a small fixed amount into savings on payday
Keep the old dining table for another year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the answer system needs testing against real bills before it takes easy chats. I would join the union meeting to ask for paid audit shifts and monthly figures on lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own hours could fall when the routine queue moves. I know the account rules, but an experienced average agent can still be one of the extra seats. With less than a month saved, the mortgage would notice a short rota immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask to test the new answer system on paid time and log false refund claims. I would take the results and my rota to the union meeting to seek paid audit practice for agents losing easy calls. In the first year, if my hours fall I would apply for a posted paid quality role only if written wages and hours cover our mortgage, and keep this job until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious and ready to test it, which is an odd combination. I can learn a new screen quickly, but I cannot manufacture a paid job from a pilot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would show wrong amounts, repeat calls and how many paid hours were used to correct them. I would not sign a good score based only on faster replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a quality course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real posted vacancy required it and the employer covered the course or we could pay without touching the mortgage money. I would ask for funding first.

I would join the **union meeting** for paid audit shifts.
think: My own **hours** could fall when routine chats move to software.
Our reserve cannot carry a shortened **mortgage wage** for more than a few weeks.

Join the **union meeting** with errors and rota.
Apply for **posted quality work** if hours fall, only with written mortgage-covering wages and hours; keep earning until signing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team AGI by 2028 could answer and check almost every call we take. I would ask the union to demand written notice, posted jobs and funded training before the roster changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my experienced desk could go quickly when full AGI reaches our screens in 2028. Robots around 2031 come later, but they do not protect a phone job. Tarek's porter wage cannot carry our mortgage and children alone, and our savings are too small for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would join the union meeting about notice and ask the manager for the names and pay of jobs that might remain. I would take funded training on paid time only if a posted role requires it; I would not buy a vague certificate from the mortgage reserve. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post ends I would apply for a paid accounts vacancy with written wages and hours covering the mortgage, and keep any current wage until a real offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the date is close and our savings are not. I can make a plan, but I cannot stretch one month of money into a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we may spend less on weekend trips while I look for work. I would keep their school routine and not hand them a prediction as if it were a fact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the only vacancy is farther away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would calculate the travel and child-care costs first. I would move only with a signed offer that leaves enough after those costs to pay the mortgage.

say: I would ask for **written notice** and posted jobs.
I would seek **funded paid-time training** through the union.
think: My screen job could end in **2028**.
Tarek’s wage and our thin **reserve** cannot carry the mortgage alone for long.
do: Join the **union meeting** on notice now.
Take funded **required training** for a posted role only on paid study time.
Seek **posted accounts work** after cuts; accept only signed wage and hours covering mortgage after travel and childcare.
S2.quote: I can make a plan, but I cannot stretch one month of money into a year.
fieldNote: She correctly separates 2028 screens from later **robots**.
Study depends on **funding** and paid time for a posted role.
Any offer must cover **mortgage, travel and childcare** costs.

steps.text: Join union meetings seeking written notice and posted paid roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues five years is enough to demand a real paid path into checking customer decisions. I would ask the union to review the jobs and wages each year, not just accept a training brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think AGI in 2031 could answer most calls, even mine. Five years lets me build audit experience while the wage still comes in, but the mortgage needs both earners. Robots around 2034 are a later concern than our screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask for a paid monthly shift checking AI answers with the quality team and learn its review method if offered. I would add small amounts to savings and attend yearly union meetings on posted audit roles. In the first year after 2031, if calls go I would apply for a paid audit vacancy only if its written wage and hours cover our mortgage; I would not leave until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but there is a route I can test. Five years gives me evidence of work I can actually do, if the centre pays for the shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count on an audit shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wrong amount, whether a customer called again and whether an agent could correct the decision. A shiny dashboard is not enough evidence for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for an audit course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted paid job required it and the employer funded the course and paid study hours. If not, I would keep learning through approved paid shifts.

S3.quote: A shiny dashboard is not enough evidence for me.
fieldNote: She counts errors and **repeat calls**, not just speed.

steps.text: Learn the quality team AI review method on paid monthly shifts if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues a decade gives time to build a paid audit job, if the centre will post one and train people. I would ask the union to keep asking where the paid hours go each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, and the mortgage may still be there. I could be working in quality review before then, but I cannot assume that desk survives full AGI either. Robots around 2039 come later than the screen change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep taking customer calls and ask to spend one paid shift a month reviewing AI decisions if the centre allows it. I would build our mortgage reserve and join the annual union meeting on hours. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if calls end I would apply for a posted paid audit job only if its written wages and hours cover the mortgage, staying in paid work until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the old queue ending, and anxious about the budget this month. A long warning helps me learn, but it does not replace wages now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you save for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full month of mortgage and household bills, then more. We are below that today, so I would not spend on a course that has no job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to stop work at 53?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have not set a date to stop earning, and I do not know the mortgage balance in 2036. I would rather build a paid skill than guess about an age.

I would have the union watch yearly **paid hours** across the contact centre.
think: I may still owe the **mortgage** at 53.
I cannot assume even **audit work** survives AGI once full thinking systems arrive.
do: Keep taking **customer calls** while they pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I know the tool well, but our mortgage does not care how curious I am. Written notice, a funded course on paid time tied to a posted job and a signed offer with enough wages and hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid to check the machine when the customer comes back. A wrong refund can survive a fast answer and still empty someone’s account.

headlineQuote: A wrong refund can survive a fast answer and still empty someone’s account.
portrait: Priya is a **43-year-old experienced** contact centre agent with secondary school education and average skill.
She has two school-age children and a mortgage with **Tarek**, and earns lower pay for her job.
She uses AI **daily**, but has less than one month saved and few nearby job options.
She seeks paid **audit work** and joins union meetings for notice, training and posted wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase her calls before the household builds even one month of reserves.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded paid-time training and a signed mortgage-covering job offer would help.
